items.title: Two Firmwares
items.stakes: Half the lobby video wall is black three days before the donor preview. Two shipments of the same decoder, two firmwares.
items.reward: One firmware, a network where the work can't touch the show — and a spec that names the version.

objectives.text: Stage the update off the show network
Decide what the spec says now

items.alt: The lobby: the video wall with every other display black; Dario, the AV contractor's project manager, points at it; Maya faces him.

bubbles.text: Two hundred and twenty took the config. A hundred and eighty said no.

items.caption: Donor preview on Friday.

lines.text: Two hundred and twenty took it. A hundred and eighty said no.
Then we find out why before anybody pushes anything else.

items.prompt: 19:15. Half the wall is black. The lighting contractor is programming the show on the same switches tonight. What now?
items.risk: A blind push beside the lighting programmer — or a black wall at the preview.

hints.text: What do you need to know before anyone changes anything?

options.label: Ask Dario to push 4.1 to all 180 right now from the production controller
options.result: Odile: “Not while my programmer is on that network.”
options.consequence: Changes production blind, next to someone else's work.

options.label: Stop pushing. Ask Dario for the controller's inventory — version and shipment per endpoint — and the network contractor for the switch and VLAN map. Nothing changes on production tonight
options.result: By nine you know which 180, why, and what else is on VLAN 60.
options.consequence: Know the split and the neighbours before touching anything.

options.label: Roll the 220 back to 3.8 so everything matches
options.result: The show config needs 4.1. Now nothing takes it.

options.label: Order 180 new decoders
options.result: Six weeks' lead time. The preview is Friday.

items.title: Two shipments, two firmwares.
items.body: The inventory: 220 decoders from shipment 1 on firmware 4.1; 180 from shipment 2, packed fourteen months earlier from a distributor's stock, on 3.8 — 45% of the fabric. The spec said ‘current firmware at delivery’. No version, no check at receiving. And the switch map has the lighting console and its nodes on VLAN 60, the AV production network — ‘temporary’ since fit-out. The drawings put lighting on VLAN 70.
items.label: Test: how much of the fabric — and what let it through?

items.sub: Advanced · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Maya and Kit beside a board. A hundred and eighty of four hundred endpoints are on three-point-eight. How long to update them safely? Forty-five percent of the fabric. Twenty at a time, six minutes a batch — nine batches, fifty-four minutes. On a staging VLAN. Not tonight, on production, while lighting programs on the same switches.

items.alt: A fabric sheet before the fix: VLAN 60 carries the controller, all 400 decoders and the lighting; VLAN 61 not built; VLAN 70 empty since fit-out; a bar of 400 decoders, 220 green on 4.1 and 180 red on 3.8, 45%; the spec line ‘current firmware at delivery’, no version named, nobody checked at receiving.
items.caption: One network, two firmwares, and a neighbour who shouldn't be there.

items.label: **Fix it:** stage the update off the show network.

items.title: One hop too far.
items.body: The network contractor builds staging VLAN 61 and moves lighting to 70, as drawn. Dario's technician takes one decoder from 3.8 to 4.1 on staging. It reboots into recovery mode. Page 3 of the release notes: anything older than 4.0 must go to 4.0 first. The 220 never took this path — they left the factory on 4.1. One decoder on a bench, not 180 on the wall.
items.label: Test: how long with two hops — and why one first?

items.prompt: 23:20. The pilot is recovered on 4.0. How do the other 179 get updated?
items.risk: A mass failure the night before the preview.
timeout: Nobody decides; the update waits a night.
The preview is a day closer.

hints.text: How do you find a problem after twenty, not after 179?

options.label: All 179 at once, through both versions, tonight
options.result: If one batch fails, it fails 179 times — the night before the preview.

options.label: Dario's team: 3.8 → 4.0 → 4.1 on staging, batches of 20, each batch checked for version, config and picture before the next — two nights, outside lighting's hours
options.result: Nine batches, two hops, six minutes each: 108 minutes over two nights. Every batch checked.
options.consequence: Staged, verified, on the maker's path.

options.label: Skip 4.0 — the 220 went straight to 4.1
options.result: Twenty more decoders in recovery mode.

options.label: Leave them on 3.8 and write a second config
options.result: Two configs to maintain for the life of the building.

items.title: Two threads
items.body: In February 1904 a fire burned through downtown Baltimore for more than a day. Engine companies came by train from Washington, Philadelphia and New York — and many of their hoses would not fit Baltimore's hydrants. The threads were different. More than 1,500 buildings were lost. A national standard for hose couplings followed within a couple of years; getting every city to adopt it took far longer.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #77 · AVERY'S LENS  A version is part of the design  If two versions of the same device behave differently, the version belongs in the specification — and gets checked when the boxes arrive.  The spec said ‘current firmware at delivery’. Two shipments arrived months apart, and ‘current’ meant two different things.

items.alt: The fabric sheet after the fix: VLAN 60 with the controller and the decoders on 4.1; VLAN 61 with the update tool and one batch of 20; VLAN 70 with the lighting console and nodes, as drawn; all 400 decoders green on 4.1; the path 3.8 to 4.0 to 4.1, 9 batches times 2 hops times 6 minutes, 108 minutes; every batch verified and the firmware register signed.
items.caption: One firmware. Nothing else touched.

items.prompt: My guys can flash all hundred and eighty tonight. Two hours. You sign off, we go.

options.label: “Not on production, not tonight. Staging VLAN first, one endpoint first — your tools, your team. I'll get the network change scheduled.”
options.reply: One first. Fine. It's cheaper than a hundred and eighty in recovery.

options.label: “Go. We need the wall.”
options.reply: …Your call. I'll want it in writing.

options.label: “Your problem, Dario. Just fix it.”
options.reply: The spec said ‘current’. That's your problem too.

items.title: fw 3.8 · 180 · ship 2
items.body: The controller's inventory, sorted by version: 220 decoders on 4.1, serials from shipment 1; 180 on 3.8, serials from shipment 2 — packed fourteen months earlier, from a distributor's warehouse.

items.prompt: Friday morning. What does the specification say from now on?
unknown: What else arrives on old stock
items.risk: The next shipment with a different ‘current’.
timeout: The spec stays as it was.
The spare decoders arrive next month — on 3.9.

hints.text: What would have caught shipment 2 at the loading dock?

options.label: A named version per device in the submittal; a version check on a sample of every shipment at receiving; a firmware register in the commissioning plan; updates pilot → batch → all, with the update path read first
options.result: Dario adds the check to his receiving form; Nkechi adds the register.
options.consequence: Name it, check it, record it.

options.label: Ban updates until opening
options.result: The next security fix waits for no one.

options.label: Blame the distributor
options.result: True, and it'll happen again with the next one.

items.label: **Service Mode:** run the three days yourself.

items.alt: The lobby at the donor preview: every display on the wall lit; Kit and Maya at either side.

bubbles.text: Four hundred of four hundred. And lighting got their VLAN back.
And the spec has a number in it where it used to say ‘current’.

items.title: Upgrade path · page 3
items.body: The 4.1 release notes, page 3, in a box nobody read: ‘Devices on versions earlier than 4.0 must be updated to 4.0 before installing 4.1. Direct updates may leave the device in recovery mode.’

items.alt: The main hall from the floor: the lighting catwalk overhead, one section unfinished behind barrier tape and a NO ACCESS sign; Odile points up at it; Maya beside her. Nobody is on the catwalk.

bubbles.text: The band rehearses Thursday. The loudspeaker cluster isn't up — and somebody's already asking about that catwalk.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Count the split before you touch it (% = part ÷ whole × 100). Stage updates on their own VLAN, away from production and its neighbours. Read the release notes for the update path, update one device first, then batches you verify (T = Σ count × time each). Name firmware versions in the spec and check them when the boxes arrive. The contractor updates; the network contractor changes the switches; Maya specifies.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Where in your work does “current” or “latest” stand in for a number someone should have written down?
